Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Elias Vance was thirty-two when the fever spiked and collapsed his lungs, leaving him in an intensive care unit for eleven days. He had come to remember the room not as a place of recovery, but as a cage of machinery and shifting air. The ventilator hissed in his chest, each breath a negotiated effort, while nurses threaded needles into his arms for IV drips that pulsed steadily, visually anchoring him to the bed. When the monitors alarmed, the sound triggered a sudden tightening behind his ribs. He did not just feel fear then; he felt horror, followed by a sharp, unplaceable guilt, as though his body had betrayed him in front of strangers. Over the following months, the hospital stayed with him. What frightened him most was not the illness itself, but the physical reactions that followed it. A simple draft from an office window could make his chest feel as though it were contracting again. He began to notice his body sitting on constant alert, shoulders braced, muscles coiled, as though waiting for another alarm. The negative emotions pooled steadily, too, lingering in the quiet hours after work. He found himself eating with rigid precision, controlling his intake strictly to feel in control. He stopped going to the gym. The prospect of pushing his heart rate felt like risking the same suffocation he had endured in the ICU. When he tried to exercise, the exertion would spark strong physical reactions—a rapid heartbeat, a flush of heat—and he would return to the couch, certain that overexertion would bring the collapse back. His work as a database administrator provided a steady rhythm, but it also became a specific site of exposure. The servers hummed at a low frequency that occasionally synced with the memory of the ICU alarms. During a critical migration project, Elias sat in his glass-walled office, watching server loads climb on his monitors. When the primary database lagged, his breathing shallowed, and his neck tightened. He had come to believe that if he did not monitor the system closely, everything would fail, just as his lungs had. The physical reactivity would flare during routine IT check-ups at the corporate clinic. He avoided the medical cues entirely, steering clear of the building, postponing physical examinations, and routing his errands to bypass the nearest hospital. He even avoided ambulances on the street, crossing to the other side of the road so he would not be caught in one. These habits accumulated quietly over weeks and months. He missed his daughter’s school recitals because the event hall’s temperature controls triggered that same chest constriction. His ex-wife, watching from a distance, noted how his restricted eating and avoided exercise had shrunk his social world, but she also saw how his avoidance made sense to him. He was not running from fear; he was managing a body that felt permanently on guard. The guilt and shame he carried were not about the illness itself, but about the way he had been so helpless in it, surrounded by needles and drips, unable to move without medical support. At thirty-seven, Elias Vance came to therapy because the rigidity had begun to wear him down. The strict control over his meals left him exhausted by dinner, and the constant alertness kept him awake. He had come to recognize that his body’s physical reactivity was no longer tied to his lungs, yet he continued to react as though every breath might fail. What he hoped for was not a return to complete health, but a loosening of the tightness that governed his days. He was most afraid of being trapped again, of that sudden breathlessness catching him when he least expected it, but he was ready to test whether the air in his office, in his life, was truly enough to keep him upright.
